topics.topic: TWO IN-CLASS QUIZZES back to back, roughly the first fifteen minutes. The VOCAB QUIZ ran on the laptop and was access-code gated - 'please don't open any other browser, okay, just a quiz. So the passcode is number one, just one' - and she told them up front how it is built: words made only of letters taught so far appear in Arabic script, and any word containing a letter not yet taught appears in TRANSLITERATION. Her advice for the transliterated ones was to sound them out silently and recognise them as words already known by ear. The WRITING QUIZ followed on paper, and she twice instructed them to write their name AND 'section 3' at the top. Mid-quiz she stopped to explain a formatting quirk in her own document: because of how Word places the marks, the tashkiil on the printed page sits with the PRECEDING letter rather than over the one it belongs to, and she walked the room through the second example letter by letter - 'don't put it on the jiim, put it on the Haa'.' A student asked whether it goes on or under, and the transcript does not capture her answer

COUNTING 0 TO 10 IN ARABIC - the substance of the hour and roughly half of it, taught as pronunciation, then handwriting, then recall under pressure. The numbers, with the Levantine (Shami) variants she gave alongside the Modern Standard forms: sifr (zero, written as a bare dot), waaHid (one - she stressed the hard H, and separately that waaHid also means 'lonely'), ithnaan/ithnayn (two, with the -ayn/-aan ending she taught as the DUAL marker in Arabic and Hebrew; Shami tnayn), thalaatha (three; Shami talaate), arba'a (four - she made them exaggerate the 'ayn because pronouncing it correctly is what will let them SPELL it correctly once 'ayn is taught; no Shami variant), khamsa (five, written as a circle, larger than a sukuun), sitta (six; Shami sitte - taught alongside the word sitt, meaning a lady), sab'a (seven, with the peace/triumph hand gesture as the mnemonic), thamaaniya (eight; Shami tamaaniye, with the losing gesture as its opposite mnemonic), tis'a (nine) and 'ashara (ten). She noted that the 'ayn appears in almost every one of them. HANDWRITING TRAPS she spent real time on: 2 and 6 are drawn in OPPOSITE directions and are 'really confusing'; the book's alternate 'two teeth' form for 2 is confusable with 3 and she recommends against it; and 9 is close enough to the English 9 to be easy. She then ran recall five separate times, calling on students by name to count from zero up to the newest number each time, and drilled the count-the-objects slides continuously

THE HISTORY OF ARABIC NUMERALS - a video plus her framing, about six minutes, which she chose to spend time on. The frame she set first: what English speakers call Arabic numerals are called HINDI or INDIC numerals in Arabic, because the Arabs adopted them from India and the West then adopted them from the Arabs. Her ruling for this course, to end the confusion: 'we're going to call English numbers English numbers and Arabic numbers Arabic numbers.' The video covered al-Khwarizmi - Persian, born in what is now Uzbekistan, working at Baghdad's House of Wisdom during the Golden Age of Islam - whose Latinised name gives us ALGORITHM and whose al-jabr gives us ALGEBRA, who corrected Ptolemy's geography with some seventy geographers under him, compiled astronomical tables later translated into Latin and Chinese, and in 825 published the work on Hindu numerals that an English monk translated three centuries later. She added the folk theory that the shapes of the English digits were built from counting the angles in each figure

HAMZA, the one new letter of the day, plus listening exercises 1, 2 and 3 on page 67 and the new vocabulary attached to them. The rule she built the whole segment on: hamza is a CONSONANT (the glottal stop) and it NEVER stands bare at the start of a word - it must have a SEAT. On alif at the beginning, where the accompanying tashkiil determines the vowel (fatHa gives a, Damma gives u, kasra gives i); on waaw; on a dotless yaa' (a 'tooth' without the two dots) in the middle; and it can sit on the line independently at the end of a word, as in shay'. Two rules she gave that are worth keeping: (1) at the beginning of a word hamza is sometimes WRITTEN and sometimes not, but it is ALWAYS PRONOUNCED - 'we cannot start a word with a vowel' - and for this class the instruction is to follow the tashkiil regardless of whether the hamza is printed; (2) the exception is the definite article al-, over which hamza is never written, and the test for whether an initial alif-hamza is part of the word is whether you can remove al- and still have a word. She also answered a student's question about why hamza plus a short vowel looks redundant: there is a real rule governing when it is written, but it is a 300-level topic. Within these exercises she taught raqm (and 'adad) for 'number', and the word list she then declared required

announcements.text: HOMEWORK IS DUE FRIDAY 2026-09-25 AND IT OPENS UNIT 4, split across two platforms - this is the detail that fills in the bare 'Homework 5' row already in the due list. 'All right, let's talk about your homework that's due this Friday... we're going to start today with a unit 4, all right? So you have to complete drill one and three. It should be submitted on Lingco... And then complete drill 2 requires you to write out a dictation and submitted on Canvas.' She restated the split a second time to be sure: 'Drill one and three on Lingco and drill 2 on Canvas writing.' Recorded below as two separate commitments precisely because a split submission is how half of an assignment gets missed.

THIS HOMEWORK IS GRADED FOR COMPLETION, NOT CORRECTNESS, AND IT CONTAINS LETTERS NOT YET TAUGHT. Her words: 'Those are new letters that we haven't learned. Maybe we will learn on Thursday'... 'whatever the homework cover, do on your own. And again, I'm not grading those for correctness, I'm grading them for completion. So any difficulty, any problem, anything wrong in the dictation, we'll address those next week.' Practical consequence: attempt everything, submit it even where it is wrong, and bring the errors to class. She judged the load herself - 'It's not too much.' Do not sink time into perfecting a dictation of letters that have not been introduced.

THURSDAY 2026-09-24 IS A SPEAKING CLASS AND SHE WILL INTRODUCE TWO NEW LETTERS: 'Thursday, I'm gonna try to speak, dedicate some time, Thursday, we'll dedicate some time to speaking, and I'll introduce 2 letters, but I don't know if the homework covers two or four of them.' She was openly unsure whether the unit 4 homework requires two letters or four, which is the reason she released the class to do what they can and defer the rest. Same shape as the 9/15 speaking-class heads-up, but note she assigned NO explicit preparation this time - no vocabulary list to review in advance was named.

NEW REQUIRED VOCABULARY FROM PAGE 67: akh (brother) and ukht (sister). She was unambiguous that these are not optional - 'they give you here the words, so I need you to learn and those are required. OK, add them to your vocabulary, brother and sister.' Also taught in the same segment, though not declared required: raqm and 'adad, both meaning 'number'; shay' (a thing), used as the end-of-word hamza example; and Saba', which she connected to the Queen of Sheba.

THE PAGE 67 LISTENING EXERCISES ARE TO BE FINISHED INDEPENDENTLY ON LINGCO, with no date attached: 'listen to those on Lingco. You could do those on your own. Do those writing exercises.' Exercises 1, 2 and 3 were started in class, all three on hamza - exercise 1 on hamza with fatHa over alif, exercise 2 on INITIAL hamza specifically, exercise 3 mixing fatHa, Damma and kasra. Deliberately kept OUT of the commitments list because she set no deadline; it is self-paced practice rather than a graded submission.

A RULE THAT WILL MATTER ON A FUTURE HOMEWORK, stated in passing while teaching 'ashara: Arabic numerals are written AND READ LEFT TO RIGHT, exactly as in English, even inside right-to-left Arabic text. 'So direction doesn't change, but the numbers, they change.' The one difference is the decimal separator - Arabic uses a COMMA where English uses a point. She attached it to a specific future task: 'If I'm asking you to write your phone number in one of the homework, write them as you write in English, but just Arabic numeral.' No such homework has been assigned yet; flagging it so it is not a surprise when it arrives.

SHE DEFENDED TEACHING SHAMI (LEVANTINE) ALONGSIDE MODERN STANDARD, unprompted, and gave a concrete payoff: a former student is applying for a Fulbright to Jordan and wrote her Levantine exposure into the application as the reason for choosing that country. 'Learning additional stuff is... I know sometimes it's hard, but it's going to be beneficial in the future if you want to apply for a government job, a scholarship, something competitive, to show that you did an extra work and you learned the dialect, that's A plus.' Consistent with the standing note that the dialect in this classroom is Levantine; today she gave Shami forms for six of the eleven numbers (tnayn, talaate, sitte, tamaaniye) and was explicit that arba'a, sab'a and tis'a do NOT change.

A FORMATTING QUIRK ON THE PRINTED WRITING QUIZ, worth knowing if it recurs on the test: because of how Word placed the marks in her document, the tashkiil on the page does not sit over the letter it belongs to but with the preceding one. She stopped the quiz to walk the room through the second example - 'So the Tashkiil goes on the previous letter, okay? So letter Tashkiil, letter Tashkiil. So when you see it, don't put it, for instance, on the [first letter]. The second example, don't put it on the jiim, put it on the Haa'.' A student immediately asked 'On or under?' and her answer is not in the recording. Marked INFERRED because the transcription is thin enough here that whether she was correcting how to READ her page or how to WRITE the mark is not fully certain - but the letter-by-letter correction she gave points at reading.

commitments.title: Homework 5, Lingco half: unit 4 drills 1 and 3, answered inside Lingco. Graded for COMPLETION, not correctness - it covers letters not yet taught, so attempt everything and bring the errors to class; she will address problems next week

Homework 5, Canvas half: unit 4 drill 2, the DICTATION - written out by hand and submitted on Canvas, not on Lingco. She stated the split twice ('Drill one and three on Lingco and drill 2 on Canvas writing') because it is easy to submit one half and miss the other. Graded for completion

position.said: 'All right, let's talk about your homework that's due this Friday... It's going to start, we're going to start today with a unit 4, all right?'... 'All right, let's do listening exercise one. That's page 67'... 'And I will see you on Thursday.' There is a real split here worth reading carefully. The HOMEWORK assigned tonight opens UNIT 4 (drills 1, 2 and 3), which is what makes unit 4 the furthest unit the class has touched. The IN-CLASS work, however, stayed inside UNIT 3 - page 67 falls in the unit 3 page range of 58-77, and the hamza listening exercises 1 through 3 are unit 3 material - alongside the numbers 0-10 and the two in-class unit 1-3 quizzes. That puts the homework roughly a week ahead of the ledger plan, which has unit 4 beginning the week of 2026-09-28. She also said plainly that the unit 4 drills contain letters she has not taught yet and that she will introduce two of them on Thursday, which is the same drift seen from the other side.

off_slide: The falafel demonstration of the Arabic L, which is a real pronunciation correction she made mid-lesson and is not on any slide: English has a deep, dark L that Americans use in 'falafel', and Arabic does not - 'It's not falafa, it's falafa. So just keep that distinction in mind because you don't want to sound like you want to try to speak like a native.' She applied it immediately to thalaatha.

Her argument for why pronunciation now determines SPELLING later, made on arba'a: if you keep saying it without the 'ayn, you will write it without the 'ayn once 'ayn is taught. 'I need you here to exaggerate the ['ayn] so you remember that there is an ['ayn]. Because later I would ask you write [arba'a].' This is the reason she kept making individual students repeat the numbers aloud rather than just recognise them.

The mnemonic system for the two numbers that sound alike: sab'a (seven) is the OPENING-UP hand gesture, read as peace in American culture and as TRIUMPH in Arabic culture (she connected it to the gesture people make saying Allahu akbar); thamaaniya (eight) is the same gesture inverted, which reads as losing or as something worse. She introduced this specifically because 'once we learn 8, they're going to be a confusion.'

The two-words-for-the-price-of-one trick on six: sitta is six, and sitt is a lady - so 'sit' and 'sit down' get you both. She added the register note that sitt is used for an older woman and mar'a is the neutral word.

Her repeated instruction on HOW to practise, given twice in different words: 'sound it in your heart' during the quiz for transliterated words, and 'if you take your packet and you start writing, say it in your heart, waaHid waaHid waaHid, ithnayn ithnayn ithnayn. That will help you also with the repetition.' Subvocalising while handwriting is the method she is actually asking for.

The dual-number aside, which is grammar rather than counting and which she slipped in while teaching two: Arabic and Hebrew both have a three-way SINGULAR / DUAL / PLURAL system, and a word ending in -ayn or -aan is dual. This is the first time the dual has come up and it is the reason ithnayn ends the way it does.

The riddle game, about three minutes, where the answer had to be given in Arabic - several of the riddles were biblical and would not be in a secular textbook: the number of days in the tomb before the resurrection (three), the days of creation in Genesis (seven), and the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23 (nine). Others were arithmetic (half of ten, fingers on one hand, fingers on two hands) and one was the number of planets, which she immediately hedged.

The shopping-basket counting game that closed the numbers block - a character named Sarah counts her purchases wrongly and the class corrects her - run through five baskets, with the class audibly getting faster by the last one.
The Ellen DeGeneres clip she recounted - a teenager handed a rotary phone and unable to work out how to dial it - prompted by the rotary phone in the count-the-objects slide for three.

A student question she answered with genuine substance and then deferred: why write a hamza at the beginning of a word when the short vowel mark above the alif already tells you the sound. Her answer - there is a rule governing when it is written, you pronounce it either way, and the rule itself waits for a 300-level course.

She opened class by passing around Arabic ketchup-flavoured chips - the most common chip flavour in the Arab world - watched the room's reaction, wrote the word out so they could pick out the taa', baa' and alif in it, and named the shop she buys them from (an Arabic grocery in Forest, which she thought was called something like 'Daily Shop Market'). She offered the rest of the bag after the quiz.
She prayed aloud before the quizzes, by name for the class and for the day's lesson on numbers, and this is a regular feature of how her class opens rather than a one-off.
terms: hamza on alif / on waaw / on dotless yaa'
the definite article al- (never takes a written hamza)
Hindi / Indic numerals vs Arabic numerals

transcription_notes: Teams could not hear Arabic at all and every number in this transcript is mangled; the forms given in this record are reconstructed from context and from the count sequences, not copied from the file. The recurring garbles: 'suffer' / 'the foot' / 'Sipper' = sifr; 'Wahel' / 'Wahad' = waaHid; 'his name' / 'it's name' / 'isnain' = ithnayn; 'Salaza' / 'the lather' / 'Bella' / 'falafa' = thalaatha; 'ARAB' (in caps, dozens of times) = arba'a; 'Samsa' / 'thumbs up' = khamsa; 'sit down' = sitta; 'Saba' / 'Sabah' = sab'a; 'the mania' / 'Femania' / 'the Mandy' = thamaaniya; 'This' / 'this style' / 'The South' = tis'a; 'Ashara' / 'I shut up' / 'Sarah' = 'ashara. Also: 'lingo' = Lingco throughout; 'Tashkir' / 'Tashki' = tashkiil; 'hands up' = hamza; 'the glot and stop' = glottal stop; 'kiss now' = kasra; 'dumba' = Damma; 'succoon' = sukuun; 'fat of' / 'Fatah' = fatHa; 'Al-Twarizmi' / 'Al Khouri Rizk me' = al-Khwarizmi; 'Golden Age of Isabel' = Golden Age of Islam. One phrase resisted reconstruction and is not relied on anywhere in this record: 'So you have to submit those in bold' at [00:20:36], which sits immediately before the correct restatement of the Lingco/Canvas split and is most likely 'in both'. The homework DUE DATE, by contrast, is unambiguous - she said 'due this Friday' twice in clean audio, and 2026-09-22 was a Tuesday.
